title: Recording of Retinal Action Potentials from Single Cells in the Insect Compound Eye
why: Copera: the second hit of the harvest query "Copera eye" (90 hits). The stored abstract says that electrical responses were recorded intracellularly from the compound eyes of a fly (Lucilia) and of several dragonflies (Copera, Agriocnemis and Lestes), describes the dragonfly ommatidium (four retinula cells and a rhabdom of three rhabdomeres) and a response of two phases, a transient spike-like potential and a slow potential maintained during illumination, and stops before the rest of the results. The full text may therefore give the time course or the flicker response of a Copera photoreceptor (cff_hz, corner_hz) or its responses to lights of different wavelengths (lambda_max_nm, spectral_range_nm). The abstract does not name the Copera species. It is the only work in the harvest or in the desk's web searches that reports a measurement on a Copera eye, and main holds no row from it. The web pairs for these traits ("Copera flicker fusion", "yellow bush dart flicker fusion", "Copera spectral sensitivity" and "yellow bush dart spectral sensitivity") returned human flicker, camera and patent pages, a Springer article (BF02160841) that earlier records on main identify as Dodt's 1954 flicker study, the van der Kooi et al. 2021 review, a darter (fish) page and records without titles (PubMed Central PMC1333798, PMC1357591 and PMC3627921, a Zoological Studies PDF in volume 31, a SOKENDAI record and an NSF record); none names a damselfly. Not opened.

title: Visual constraints upon avian behaviour
why: Ptilinopus: a Cardiff PhD thesis on how avian behaviour is constrained by eye design, using eye size, retinal image brightness and retinal topography across bird species (stored abstract). The harvest listed it as the one hit of "Ptilinopus spectral sensitivity opsin", first of five for "Ptilinopus visual acuity" and third of 107 for "Ptilinopus visual field"; OpenAlex can match words in a full text, so the thesis may name a fruit dove in its species comparisons, and its eye-size or retinal-topography data may give an acuity or a receptor spacing (acuity_cpd, interreceptor_deg) or bear on the visual field (fov_h_deg, binocular_deg) of a Ptilinopus species. The stored abstract start names no species. Main's wanted list harvest-37 holds the same thesis for Pooecetes and Oriolus. The acuity pair ("Ptilinopus visual acuity", "fruit dove visual acuity") returned a species-recognition preprint, the Wikipedia page on fruit doves, a patent, grasshopper and penguin vision papers, the colour-sensitivity preprint named above, Caves et al. 2024 (main holds 607 rows over 143 taxa from it, whose doves are Columba livia and Zenaida macroura), a Springer article (10.1007/s00359-020-01404-y) and Duke, Kansas and Bundaberg pages without titles, a Renewables Grid Initiative file by Martin titled Birds eye view and blogs on dove vision; none names a fruit dove measurement. The visual-field pair ("Ptilinopus visual field", "fruit dove visual field") returned Wikipedia and BirdForum pages on fruit doves, velvet worm, zebrafish and biting-fly papers, the owl binocular-field study of Potier et al. 2023, the seabird visual-field study of Lucas et al. 2024, a PubMed Central record (PMC5682009) and an Acta Zoologica Bulgarica PDF of 2021 without titles, a butterfly visual-field study, birding-list and eBird pages and a zoo page; none names a fruit dove visual field. Not opened.
get: green open access (Cardiff ORCA PDF from the harvest listing): http://orca.cf.ac.uk/55002/1/U585391.pdf

title: The Various Ways in Which Birds Blink
why: Ptilinopus: a hit of the harvest query "Ptilinopus visual acuity" (5 hits), so its text probably names a fruit dove. The stored abstract describes video recordings of blinking in 591 bird species from 125 families and says that nictitating-membrane blinks were rapid and occurred mainly on head movement, so its species table may say whether a Ptilinopus species makes saccadic head movements or bobs its head (eye_movement). The same paper is on main's wanted list for Chalcophaps (harvest-41), where an audit found that its Table A1 gives each species' blink type. The eye-movement pair ("Ptilinopus eye movement", "fruit dove eye movement") returned gaze-stabilization papers on mantis shrimps, eye-tracking, oculomotor and blink-MRI papers, patents, a 1973 Nature PDF without a title, the Wikipedia page on the superb fruit dove, Moore et al. 2017 on head and eye movements of foveate birds (main logs its 32 taxa, whose doves are Columba livia and Zenaida macroura), eBird and birding pages and a database of human eye movements; none names a fruit dove measurement. Not opened.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE GECKO FOVEA: CHRONICLING AND CHARACTERIZING BODY AND RETINAL MORPHOGENESIS IN A NEW LIZARD MODEL, PHELSUMA LATICAUDA
why: Phelsuma: a 2026 thesis returned by the harvest queries "Phelsuma vision" (fourth of 172 hits) and "Phelsuma eye". Its title says it characterizes the body and retinal morphogenesis of the fovea in Phelsuma laticauda, the queue's species with the most records, and its stored abstract opens on the fovea as the retinal region with the highest density of cone photoreceptors that gives high-acuity vision, so the thesis may give the cone density of the adult fovea or an acuity for P. laticauda (acuity_cpd), and it may describe the adult eye and its pupil (pupil_shape). Main holds no row from it. The acuity pair ("Phelsuma visual acuity", "day gecko visual acuity") returned the bioRxiv preprint on colour and attention to images in geckos, the Wikidata entry for the paper on the fine structure of the cone of Phelsuma inunguis, a patent, the Wikipedia and EcuRed pages, Caves et al. 2024 on birds, a Semantic Scholar topic page, a mammal retina preprint, an AskNature page on gecko pupils, the PubMed page of Roth et al. 2009, an SICB page, a Science Japan news item, the Rhoptropus afer locomotion paper and its Inside JEB note, a Science News Explores story on gecko night vision, and a Lund University record, a PubMed Central record (PMC1810110) and a Springer article (BF00362521) without titles; none names a day gecko acuity. title: The pupils and optical systems of gecko eyes
why: Phelsuma: a hit of the harvest query "Phelsuma vision" (tenth of 172 hits), and the screen tool's one candidate for pupil_shape. Its title promises the pupils of gecko eyes, and main's rows from its abstract (evidence/oa-3.jsonl line 492; audit/corrected/herps.jsonl line 65) say that it compares the multifocal helmet gecko with the day gecko Phelsuma madagascariensis grandis, whose optical system is monofocal; the full text should describe the day gecko's pupil (pupil_shape), which rule 3 carries within the genus, and it may give an optical resolution (acuity_cpd). Main read the abstract only, and its source note (sources/oa-none-3.jsonl) found no readable free copy, although the harvest lists the journal as gold open access. Main's wanted list sweep-50 holds it for the same six species. The pupil pair ("Phelsuma pupil shape", "day gecko pupil shape") returned a PubMed Central table (PMC3233692) without a title, the Plazi treatment of the original description of Phelsuma borai (Glaw, Köhler and Vences 2009), Wikipedia pages on two day geckos, a preprint on amphibian pupil shapes, zoo pages on day geckos (Paris, Perth, the National Zoo), a BioStor file (biostor-97885) without a title, a patent, a Danish encyclopedia entry on day geckos, an AskNature page, a Nautilus essay on pupil shapes, the PubMed page of Roth et al. 2009 and a CORE copy of Banks et al. 2015 (canon, in hand; main holds 461 rows over 232 taxa from it and no Phelsuma); a species description or a zoo page may state the pupil of a day gecko, and none was opened. Not opened.

title: Morphological traits of the eyes of Lepidoptera indicate selection for binocular vision in both diurnal butterflies and nocturnal moths
why: A preprint on the eye morphology of 2,730 specimens of 224 butterfly and moth species, sampled across a tribal-level phylogeny of butterflies and a genomic sampling of moths, which links eye features to detectability, resolution and stereopsis; its stored abstract start names no species, so whether its species list or data hold a species of these genera, and whether they give an acuity or an interommatidial angle (acuity_cpd, interommatidial_deg), is unseen. Main has logged eye-type, depth-cue and diel rows from its text and no acuity or angle, and several of main's wanted lists already hold it for other Lepidoptera. For this unit: Hesperia: the harvest's Hesperiidae vision review returned it (stored abstract start, no species named); the acuity pair ("Hesperia visual acuity", "branded skipper visual acuity") returned a French dictionary entry, patents, human acuity studies, the Wikipedia and StatPearls pages, Bologna and Tübingen catalogue records without titles and pages on vision in skiing and sport, and none names a skipper; Melipotis: the harvest did not list it for this genus, whose Erebidae review printed other works; the moths of the preprint come from a genomic sampling whose species are unseen, and the acuity pair ("Melipotis visual acuity", "indomitable melipotis visual acuity") returned the Wikipedia page on Melipotis indomita, velvet worm and millipede eye papers, an arXiv method for charting compound-eye fields, a patent, Springer and PubMed Central records without titles (10.1007/s00359-016-1118-8, PMC5023731) and pages on the desert ant Melophorus, which the search matched on a similar name; none names a Melipotis measurement. Not opened.
